figures.name: Mor Aphrem (Ephrem the Syrian)
figures.description: Theologian, poet, and hymnographer. Wrote extensively in Syriac and is considered one of the greatest Aramean literary figures.

figures.name: Mor Yaqub of Serugh
figures.description: Prolific Syriac poet and bishop, known for his metrical homilies. Wrote over 760 verse homilies in Syriac.

figures.name: Bar Hebraeus (Mor Gregorios Abu al-Faraj)
figures.description: Maphrian of the Syriac Orthodox Church, polymath, historian, and theologian. Wrote in Syriac and Arabic on theology, philosophy, grammar, and history.

figures.name: Hazael
figures.description: King of Aram-Damascus who expanded the kingdom to its greatest territorial extent, defeating Israel and Judah.

figures.name: Abgar V Ukama
figures.description: Aramean king of Osroene (Edessa/Urhoy). According to tradition, corresponded with Jesus and was healed by the Apostle Thaddeus.

figures.name: Mor Michael Rabo (Michael the Great)
figures.description: Syriac Orthodox Patriarch of Antioch and author of the largest surviving Syriac historical work, the Chronicle.

figures.name: Nabopolassar
figures.description: Chaldean (Kaldu-Aramean) general who founded the Neo-Babylonian Empire and destroyed the Assyrian Empire.

figures.name: Nebuchadnezzar II
figures.description: King of the Neo-Babylonian (Chaldean) Empire. Built the Hanging Gardens and expanded the empire to its greatest extent.

figures.name: Mor Yaqub Burd'ono (Jacob Baradaeus)
figures.description: Syriac Orthodox bishop who revived the Miaphysite church by ordaining clergy across the Near East. The Syriac Orthodox Church is sometimes called 'Jacobite' after him.

figures.name: Bardaisan (Bar Daysan)
figures.description: Philosopher, scientist, and poet from Edessa. One of the earliest Syriac writers, known for his hymns and cosmological works.

figures.name: Tatian the Assyrian
figures.description: Aramean theologian who composed the Diatessaron, a harmony of the four Gospels in Syriac that was widely used in the Syriac-speaking church.

figures.name: Zenobia
figures.description: Queen of the Palmyrene Empire who briefly conquered Egypt and much of the Roman East. Ruled from the Aramean city of Palmyra.

figures.name: Mor Aphrem Barsoum
figures.description: Syriac Orthodox Patriarch of Antioch and scholar. Authored 'The Scattered Pearls', a history of Syriac literature and sciences.

figures.name: Naim Faiq
figures.description: Aramean journalist and activist who advocated for Aramean national identity. Published the newspaper 'Kawkab Madnho' (Star of the East).

figures.name: Lucian of Samosata
figures.description: Satirist and rhetorician from Samosata (Commagene). Wrote in Greek but identified himself as an Aramean ('Syrian barbarian').

figures.name: Hezion
figures.description: Founder of the Aram-Damascus dynasty (biblical).

figures.name: Tabrimmon
figures.description: Son of Hezion, king of Aram-Damascus.

figures.name: Ben-Hadad I
figures.description: King of Aram-Damascus who allied with Asa of Judah against Israel.

figures.name: Hadadezer
figures.description: King of Aram-Damascus who led the anti-Assyrian coalition at the Battle of Qarqar (853 BC).

figures.name: Ben-Hadad III
figures.description: Son of Hazael. Under his reign, Aram-Damascus declined in power.

figures.name: Hadianu
figures.description: King of Aram-Damascus known from Assyrian sources. Shamshi-ilu reports taking booty from his palace.

figures.name: Rezin
figures.description: Last king of Aram-Damascus. Conquered by Tiglath-Pileser III in 732 BC.

figures.name: Hadadezer of Zobah
figures.description: King of Aram-Zobah, defeated by David of Israel (2 Samuel 8).

figures.name: Talmai
figures.description: King of Geshur and father-in-law of David (2 Samuel 3:3).

figures.name: Toi (Tou)
figures.description: King of Hamath, contemporary of David. Sent gifts after the defeat of Hadadezer of Zobah.

figures.name: Hadoram
figures.description: Son of Toi; sent by his father to congratulate David on his victory over Hadadezer (2 Samuel 8:10).

figures.name: Paratas
figures.description: King of Hamath; attested in the period between Toi's dynasty and Urhilina.

figures.name: Urhilina
figures.description: King of Hamath and father of Irhuleni. Known from Assyrian sources.

figures.name: Irhuleni
figures.description: King of Hamath who led a coalition against Assyria at the Battle of Qarqar.

figures.name: Uratamis
figures.description: King of Hamath attested between Irhuleni and Zakkur.

figures.name: Zakkur
figures.description: King of Hamath and Lu'ash. Erected the Zakkur Stele commemorating his victory over a coalition led by Bar-Hadad.

figures.name: Eni-Ilu
figures.description: King of Hamath attested between Zakkur and Yaubi'di.

figures.name: Yaubi'di
figures.description: Last king of Hamath who led a revolt against Assyria. Defeated and executed by Sargon II.

figures.name: Gusi
figures.description: Founder of the Bit-Agusi dynasty.

figures.name: Hadram
figures.description: Son of Gusi, also known as Arame in Assyrian sources.

figures.name: Attar-šumki I
figures.description: Son of Hadram, also known as Bar-Guš. Vassal of Adad-nirari III.

figures.name: Bar-Hadad
figures.description: Son of Attar-šumki I; brief reign.

figures.name: Attar-šumki II
figures.description: Son of Bar-Hadad; ruled Bit-Agusi before Mati'el.

figures.name: Mati'el
figures.description: Last independent king of Bit-Agusi. Party to the Sefire treaties. Defeated by Tiglath-Pileser III after a three-year siege.

figures.name: Adin
figures.description: Founder of Bit-Adini, after whom the kingdom was named.

figures.name: Ahuni
figures.description: Son of Adin. Last king of Bit-Adini. Defeated and deported by Shalmaneser III.

figures.name: Gabbar
figures.description: Founder of the Bit-Gabbar dynasty at Sam'al.

figures.name: Bamah
figures.description: Son of Gabbar; second ruler of the dynasty at Sam'al.

figures.name: Hayya
figures.description: Son of Bamah; ruler of Sam'al.

figures.name: Sha'il
figures.description: Son of Hayya; listed in the Kilamuwa inscription.

figures.name: Kilamuwa
figures.description: Brother of Sha'il. King of Bit-Gabbar who erected the Kilamuwa Stele.

figures.name: Qarli
figures.description: Unified Sam'al and Y'DY. Father of Panamuwa I.

figures.name: Panamuwa I
figures.description: Son of Qarli. King of Bit-Gabbar who erected the Hadad statue inscription in Samalian Aramaic.

figures.name: Bar-Sur
figures.description: Usurper who seized the throne of Bit-Gabbar.

figures.name: Panamuwa II
figures.description: Restored to the throne by Tiglath-Pileser III. Died during the Assyrian campaign against Damascus.

figures.name: Bar-Rakib
figures.description: Last king of Bit-Gabbar. Loyal Assyrian vassal who left multiple inscriptions.

figures.name: Bahianu
figures.description: Dynasty founder of Bit-Bahiani, the nomadic Aramean tribe chief after whom the kingdom was named.

figures.name: Abisalmu
figures.description: Successor of Bahianu; early ruler of Bit-Bahiani at Guzana.

figures.name: Kapara
figures.description: Ruler of Bit-Bahiani who built the famous palace at Tell Halaf (Guzana).

figures.name: Hadad-yis'i
figures.description: Aramean governor of Guzana known from the Tell Fekheriye bilingual inscription dedicated to the storm god Hadad.

figures.name: Ammi-Ba'al
figures.description: King of Bit-Zamani, known for his conflicts with Tukulti-Ninurta II of Assyria.

figures.name: Bur-Ramman
figures.description: Successor of Ammi-Ba'al as king of Bit-Zamani.

figures.name: Ilan
figures.description: Brother of Bur-Ramman; last known king of Bit-Zamani before Assyrian conquest.

figures.name: Merodach-Baladan II
figures.description: Chaldean/Aramean leader who twice seized the throne of Babylon and allied with Elam against Assyria.

figures.name: Aryu
figures.description: The founding ruler of the Abgarid dynasty of Osroene.

figures.name: Abdu
figures.description: Son of Maz'ur; second king of the dynasty.

figures.name: Fradasht
figures.description: Son of Gebar'u; early ruler of the kingdom.

figures.name: Bakru I
figures.description: Son of Fradasht; ruled during the early formative years of Osroene.

figures.name: Bakru II
figures.description: Son of Bakru I; ruled independently before sharing power with co-regents.

figures.name: Ma'nu I
figures.description: Ruled jointly alongside Bakru II for a brief period.

figures.name: Abgar I Piqa
figures.description: Surnamed 'The Dumb'. Initially co-ruled with Bakru II before reigning alone. The first historical king to bear the name Abgar.

figures.name: Abgar II
figures.description: Son of Abgar I. Dealt extensively with the Romans under Pompey and Crassus during his reign.

figures.name: Ma'nu II
figures.description: Surnamed 'Aloho' (The God). Took the throne following a brief one-year interregnum.

figures.name: Paqor
figures.description: Ruled Osroene during a period heavily influenced by regional Roman-Parthian conflicts.

figures.name: Abgar III
figures.description: Third ruler to bear the dynastic name Abgar.

figures.name: Abgar IV Sumaqa
figures.description: Surnamed 'The Red'; held a brief three-year reign over the city-state.

figures.name: Ma'nu III Saflul
figures.description: Maintained a stable multi-decade rule prior to the dawn of the common era.

figures.name: Abgar V Ukama (1st Tenure)
figures.description: Aramean king of Osroene (Edessa/Urhoy). Surnamed 'The Black'. His first period on the throne.

figures.name: Ma'nu IV
figures.description: Son of Ma'nu III; briefly interrupted the rule of Abgar V.

figures.name: Abgar V Ukama (2nd Tenure)
figures.description: Returned to power for a highly celebrated second reign. Famous in Christian tradition for his legendary correspondence with Jesus.

figures.name: Ma'nu V
figures.description: Son of Abgar V; succeeded his father following his death.

figures.name: Ma'nu VI
figures.description: Another son of Abgar V who succeeded his brother Ma'nu V.

figures.name: Abgar VI
figures.description: Son of Ma'nu VI; his death led to a long multi-decade interregnum in the kingdom.

figures.name: Abgar VII
figures.description: Son of Ezad. Ruled during Roman Emperor Trajan’s campaigns in Mesopotamia and was eventually deposed by Rome.

figures.name: Yalur
figures.description: Ruled jointly alongside the Roman puppet king Parthamaspates following a period of chaos.

figures.name: Ma'nu VII
figures.description: Son of Ezad; restored the native Abgarid dynastic line to power with Roman approval.

figures.name: Ma'nu VIII (1st Tenure)
figures.description: Son of Ma'nu VII. His first reign ended when he was temporarily driven out by the Parthians.

figures.name: Wa'el
figures.description: Son of Sahru. A rival king placed on the throne of Edessa as a proxy for the Parthian Empire.

figures.name: Ma'nu VIII (2nd Tenure)
figures.description: Restored to his throne by the Romans after they drove the Parthians out of Upper Mesopotamia.

figures.name: Abgar VIII the Great
figures.description: Son of Ma'nu VIII. One of the most famous rulers of Edessa; oversaw a massive cultural flourishing of Syriac literature and art.

figures.name: Abgar IX Severus
figures.description: Son of Abgar VIII. Summoned and deposed by Roman Emperor Caracalla, effectively ending Osroene's true independence.

figures.name: Ma'nu IX
figures.description: Ruled primarily in name only under direct Roman oversight and provincial administrative status.

figures.name: Abgar X Frahad
figures.description: Son of Ma'nu IX; the final nominal ruler of the historic Abgarid dynasty before complete Roman provincial integration.

figures.name: Mor Philoxenos of Mabbug
figures.description: Bishop of Mabbug (Hierapolis) and prolific Syriac theologian. Commissioned a major revision of the Syriac Bible.

figures.name: Mor Dionysius bar Salibi
figures.description: Syriac Orthodox bishop and encyclopedic writer. Authored commentaries on the Bible, liturgy, and theology in Syriac.

figures.name: Ahiqar
figures.description: Aramean sage and chancellor to the Assyrian kings Sennacherib and Esarhaddon. His wisdom proverbs were widely circulated in the ancient Near East.

figures.name: Mor Shimun of Beth Arsham
figures.description: Bishop and diplomat known as 'the Persian Debater'. Defended Miaphysite theology and wrote letters documenting the persecution of Christians in Yemen.

figures.name: Sergius of Resh'aina
figures.description: Physician and translator who rendered Greek philosophical and medical works into Syriac, bridging Greek and Aramean intellectual traditions.

figures.name: Mor Philoxenos Yuhanon Dolabani
figures.description: Syriac Orthodox Archbishop of Mardin. Prolific scholar, educator, and writer who authored 69 books and preserved Syriac manuscripts and heritage.

figures.name: Theophilus of Edessa
figures.description: Maronite astrologer, historian, and translator. Served as court astrologer to the Abbasid caliph al-Mahdi and wrote historical chronicles in Syriac.

figures.name: Mor Yaqub of Edessa
figures.description: Bishop, grammarian, and polymath. Revised the Syriac Old Testament and wrote extensively on grammar, philosophy, and canon law.

figures.name: Shmuel Dawid
figures.description: Aramean educator and cultural activist in the Ottoman Empire. Founded schools and worked to preserve Syriac language and identity.

figures.name: Ashur Yusuf
figures.description: Journalist, writer, and teacher in Diyarbakır who promoted Aramean cultural awareness. Killed during the Sayfo genocide in 1915.

figures.name: Mor Ignatius Zakka I Iwas
figures.description: Syriac Orthodox Patriarch of Antioch (1980-2014). Scholar and linguist who authored works on Syriac grammar and church history.

figures.name: Mor Ignatius Ya'qub III
figures.description: Syriac Orthodox Patriarch of Antioch who led the church through a period of diaspora and modernization after World War II.

figures.name: Israel Audo
figures.description: Chaldean Catholic Bishop of Mardin. Documented the Sayfo genocide and worked to protect his community during World War I.

figures.name: Toma Audo
figures.description: Chaldean Catholic Archbishop of Urmia and lexicographer. Compiled the comprehensive Syriac-Syriac dictionary 'Simta d-Leshana Suryaya'.

figures.name: Narsai
figures.description: Syriac poet and theologian known as 'the Harp of the Spirit'. Headed the School of Nisibis and composed over 360 metrical homilies.

figures.name: Thabbith bar Qurra
figures.description: Mathematician, astronomer, and physician from Harran. Translated Greek scientific works into Syriac and Arabic and made original contributions to mathematics.

figures.name: Mor Gregorios Yuhanna Ibrahim
figures.description: Syriac Orthodox Archbishop of Aleppo. Kidnapped in 2013 while on a humanitarian mission; widely regarded as a martyr for peace.

figures.name: Theodora
figures.description: Empress of the Byzantine Empire as wife of Justinian I. Of Aramean origin from Syria, she was a key protector of the Miaphysite Syriac Christians and sheltered persecuted clergy.

figures.name: Mor Yuhannon of Tella
figures.description: Bishop of Tella who ordained thousands of priests and deacons to preserve the Syriac Orthodox Church during severe Chalcedonian persecution. Martyred in 538 AD.

figures.name: Mor Severus of Antioch
figures.description: Syriac Orthodox Patriarch of Antioch (512-518) and leading Miaphysite theologian. His extensive Syriac writings shaped the theology of the Syriac Orthodox Church.

figures.name: Rabbula of Edessa
figures.description: Bishop of Edessa (411-435). Reformed the Syriac church, promoted the Peshitta Bible translation, and championed Cyrilline Christology against Nestorius.

figures.name: Balai of Qenneshrin
figures.description: Syriac poet and chorepiscopos from the region of Aleppo. Invented the five-syllable meter in Syriac poetry. His hymns became part of the Syriac liturgy.

figures.name: Shimun Quqoyo (Simeon the Potter)
figures.description: Syriac poet known for his dramatic dialogic poems (sogyotho). His verse dialogues on biblical themes are among the finest in Syriac literature.

figures.name: Marutha of Maypherqat
figures.description: Bishop of Martyropolis (Maypherqat). Diplomat between Rome and Persia who helped reorganize the Church of the East and collected relics of Persian martyrs.

figures.name: Daniel of Salah
figures.description: Syriac biblical exegete, theologian, and abbot. Authored extensive commentaries on the Psalms and other biblical books in Syriac.

figures.name: Simeon the Stylite
figures.description: Aramean ascetic who lived atop a pillar near Aleppo for 37 years. One of the most famous saints in the early church, attracting pilgrims from across the known world.

figures.name: Cyrillona (Qurilona)
figures.description: Early Syriac poet from the Edessa region. A younger contemporary of Ephrem, ranked among the foremost early Syriac poets for his six surviving poems on biblical and liturgical themes.

figures.name: Isaac of Antioch
figures.description: Prolific Syriac writer and priest, author of numerous metrical homilies distinguished by their originality and acumen. One of the stars of classical Syriac literature.

figures.name: Mushe bar Kepha
figures.description: One of the most celebrated Syriac Orthodox bishops and writers of the 9th century. Authored commentaries on Scripture, liturgy, and philosophy in Syriac.

figures.name: Giwargi, Bishop of the Arabs
figures.description: Syriac Orthodox bishop and polymath steeped in Greek philosophy. His Syriac writings on theology, philosophy, and Aristotelian logic are important sources for Syriac intellectual history.

figures.name: Eliya of Nisibis
figures.description: Archbishop of Nisibis and scholar. Authored a Syriac-Arabic chronicle, a Syriac grammar, and interfaith dialogues between Christianity and Islam.

figures.name: Yuhannon bar Madon
figures.description: Syriac poet from Bartella, known for his religious poems and hymns (sugitho). A representative of the Syriac literary tradition in the Mosul region.

figures.name: Khamis bar Qardahe
figures.description: East Syriac poet and grammarian from Arbela. Authored a collection of hymns and poems, and a Syriac grammar. One of the last major classical Syriac poets.

figures.name: Mor Quryaqos of Tagrit
figures.description: Syriac Orthodox Maphrian of the East and author of hymns and theological works. Important figure in the Syriac literary tradition of the Abbasid period.

figures.name: Babai the Great
figures.description: East Syriac monk and theologian who led the Church of the East during an interregnum. Authored major Christological works and monastic rules in Syriac.

figures.name: Isaac of Nineveh
figures.description: Bishop and mystic of the Church of the East, renowned for his Syriac writings on asceticism and prayer. His works were translated into Greek, Arabic, and many other languages.

figures.name: Yuhannon of Ephesus (John of Ephesus)
figures.description: Syriac Orthodox bishop and historian. Authored an Ecclesiastical History and Lives of the Eastern Saints documenting Miaphysite communities across the Near East.

figures.name: Giwargis Warda
figures.description: East Syriac poet from Arbela. His collection of hymns (Warda, 'Rose') is one of the most important collections of later medieval Syriac poetry.

figures.name: Abdisho bar Brikha
figures.description: Metropolitan of Nisibis and last great writer of classical East Syriac literature. Composed the Metrical Catalogue of Syriac Authors, theological works, and the poem Paradise of Eden.

figures.name: Athanasius of Balad
figures.description: Syriac Orthodox Patriarch of Antioch and scholar of the monastery of Qenneshre. Translated Greek philosophical and scientific works into Syriac.

figures.name: Ahudemmeh
figures.description: Miaphysite bishop and missionary who evangelized Arab tribes in Mesopotamia. Martyred by the Sasanian authorities for converting Persians to Christianity.

figures.name: Sahdona (Martyrius)
figures.description: East Syriac monk and mystical writer. Authored the Book of Perfection, a major work on the spiritual life and contemplative prayer in Syriac.

figures.name: Denha I
figures.description: Patriarch of the Church of the East during the Mongol period. Engaged in diplomacy with the Mongol Ilkhanate and Western Christian powers.

figures.name: Thomas of Marga
figures.description: East Syriac bishop and historian. Authored the Book of Governors, a history of the monasteries of Beth Abe and their leaders in northern Mesopotamia.

figures.name: Shubhalmaran of Beth Qatraye
figures.description: East Syriac bishop and author of theological commentaries. Part of the Beth Qatraye school of scholars in the Persian Gulf region.

figures.name: Gewargis of Beltan
figures.description: Syriac Orthodox Patriarch of Antioch (758-789). Trained at the monastery of Qenneshre in Greek and Syriac philology, theology, and jurisprudence.

figures.name: Yuhannon of Dalyatha
figures.description: East Syriac monk and one of the greatest Syriac mystical writers. His letters and discourses on prayer, contemplation, and divine vision influenced Eastern Christian spirituality.

figures.name: Yosep Hazzaya
figures.description: East Syriac mystic and theologian. Authored treatises on the spiritual life describing stages of purification, illumination, and perfection in Syriac.

figures.name: Dionysius of Tel Mahre
figures.description: Syriac Orthodox Patriarch of Antioch (818-845) and historian. Authored a major chronicle covering events from 582 to 842 AD, used as a source by later Syriac historians.

figures.name: Joshua the Stylite
figures.description: Syriac chronicler from Edessa who documented the Roman-Persian wars, plague, and famine in Mesopotamia between 494-506 AD. One of the most vivid firsthand accounts in Syriac literature.

figures.name: Mor Quryaqos of Amid
figures.description: Syriac Orthodox Patriarch of Antioch. Known for his efforts to consolidate the church and his correspondence with other Christian leaders.

figures.name: Mor Ignatius Ni'matullah
figures.description: Syriac Orthodox Patriarch of Antioch during the Ottoman period. Maintained the church through difficult times and engaged with Catholic missions.

figures.name: Shlemon of Basra
figures.description: East Syriac author of The Book of the Bee, an encyclopedic work on biblical history, theology, and cosmology written in Syriac.

figures.name: Hananya of Adiabene
figures.description: East Syriac author who wrote on logic and philosophy. Part of the Nisibis school tradition of translating and commenting on Greek philosophical works in Syriac.

figures.name: Yokhannan bar Penkaye
figures.description: East Syriac monk and historian. Authored the Ktaba d-Resh Melle, a universal history that is a vital source for the early Islamic conquest of Mesopotamia from a Syriac Christian perspective.

figures.name: Simeon of Beth Arsham
figures.description: Bishop and diplomat known as 'the Persian Debater'. Defended Miaphysite theology and wrote letters documenting the persecution of Christians in Najran, Yemen.

figures.name: Hnanisho I
figures.description: Catholicos-Patriarch of the Church of the East (685-700). Oversaw the church during the early Umayyad period and promoted monastic reform.

figures.name: Timotheos I
figures.description: Catholicos-Patriarch of the Church of the East (780-823). One of the most important leaders of the church, known for his letters, apologetics, and expansion of missions to Central Asia and China.

figures.name: Yuhannon bar Kipho
figures.description: First Maphrian (Catholicos) of Tagrit, establishing the office that would lead the Syriac Orthodox Church in the East for centuries.

figures.name: Gabriel of Beth Rabban
figures.description: Director of the School of Nisibis and East Syriac teacher of biblical interpretation. Continued the scholarly tradition of the most important Syriac academic institution.

figures.name: Severus bar Mashqo
figures.description: Syriac Orthodox Patriarch of Antioch (667-681). A monk from the convent of Dayro da-Pgimto who led the church during the early Umayyad period.

figures.name: Abraham Nahshirtono
figures.description: Syriac Orthodox Maphrian of the East and liturgical author. Composed an Anaphora (eucharistic prayer) that remains part of Syriac liturgical tradition.

figures.name: Peter Barsymes
figures.description: Aramean from Syria who served as Praetorian Prefect of the East under Emperor Justinian - one of the highest administrative positions in the Byzantine Empire.

figures.name: Magnus
figures.description: Aramean of Syrian origin who served as Roman general and high official under emperors Justin II and Tiberius. Campaigned against the Persians in the 570s in the eastern frontier.

figures.name: Antoninus I
figures.description: Syrian Syriac Orthodox bishop ordained by Jacob Baradaeus. Participated in the creation of Peter as Miaphysite patriarch of Alexandria in 575.

figures.name: Antoninus II
figures.description: Syrian Syriac Orthodox bishop ordained by Jacob Baradaeus. Participated alongside his namesake in the creation of Peter as patriarch of Alexandria in 575.

figures.name: Bar Nbyl
figures.description: Monastic head of the monastery of Fytr. Teacher of the saint Habib.

figures.name: Theophilus Bar Ma'nu
figures.description: Aramean presbyter from Tella and father of Jacob Baradaeus, the reviver of the Syriac Orthodox Church.

figures.name: Hassan Bar Bahlul
figures.description: Syriac Orthodox lexicographer who compiled the Lexicon Syriacum, the most comprehensive Syriac-Arabic dictionary of the medieval period. A landmark of Syriac scholarship.

figures.name: Clemens Joseph David
figures.description: Syriac Catholic Archbishop of Damascus (1879-1890). Scholar who collected Syriac manuscripts and published works on Syriac literature and church history.

figures.name: Abraham Yohannan
figures.description: Syriac philologist, historian, and the first Oriental to teach Oriental languages at Columbia University. Identified Syriacs as originally Aramean (Armoye) and published on Syriac language and literature.

figures.name: Paul Al-Khoury Al-Kfarnissy
figures.description: Maronite scholar and professor of Syriac at the Lebanese Maronite Order. Authored a grammar of the Aramaic Syriac language and a history of Syriac literature.

figures.name: Abd al-Masih Nu'man Qarabashi
figures.description: Syriac Orthodox educator and writer from Tur Abdin. Authored works on Syriac grammar and documented the massacres of Syriac Christians in Turkey in 1895 and 1914-1918.

figures.name: Timotheos Isaac bar ʿBed Hayyo
figures.description: Syriac Orthodox Maphrian (head of the eastern branch of the Syriac Orthodox Church).

figures.name: Jacob bar Shakko
figures.description: Syriac Orthodox scholar from Bartella. Authored works on philosophy, theology, dialectics, and Syriac grammar. A leading figure of the Syriac Renaissance.

figures.name: Gabriel ibn al-Qila'i
figures.description: Maronite poet and historian from Lebanon. Wrote in Syriac (Garshuni) and Arabic, defending Maronite identity and composing historical and religious verse.

figures.name: Yuhannon of Dara
figures.description: Syriac Orthodox archimandrite of the monastery of Qartmin in Tur Abdin and bishop of Dara. Close companion of Jacob Baradaeus on his final journey to Egypt.

figures.name: Sabrisho of Beth Garmai
figures.description: East Syriac metropolitan of Beth Garmai who established the Fast of Nineveh (Ba'uta d-Ninwaye), a three-day fast still observed in Syriac Christian tradition today.

figures.name: Sa'id bar Sabouni
figures.description: Syriac Orthodox metropolitan of Melitene. Authored theological and polemical works in Syriac during the period of the Syriac Renaissance.

figures.name: Habib Abu Ra'ita of Tagrit
figures.description: Syriac Orthodox theologian from Tagrit and one of the earliest Arabic-writing Christian apologists. Defended Miaphysite Christology against Muslims and rival Christian denominations.

figures.name: Constantine of Edessa
figures.description: Disciple of Jacob of Edessa and Syriac Orthodox bishop of Emesa and later Edessa. Participated in the Synod of Manazgirt (726) and was a monk at the Monastery of Eusebona.

figures.name: Yuhannon the Stylite of Litarba
figures.description: Monk, stylite, and author from Litarba near Aleppo. One of the Syriac literary figures of the 8th century.

figures.name: Aba of Kashkar
figures.description: East Syriac polymath, author, and diplomat active during the reigns of Shah Khusrau II of Persia and Emperor Maurice of Byzantium.

figures.name: Sergius al-Rizzi
figures.description: Maronite bishop of Damascus, author, and scholar involved in the printing of Syriac and Arabic texts in Rome. From an influential family - two uncles and a brother were Maronite patriarchs.

figures.name: Peter Makhluf
figures.description: Maronite cleric, scholar, and bishop of Cyprus. Secretary to Patriarch al-Duwayhi, involved in the printing, revision, and translation of the Maronite breviary in Rome.

figures.name: Abd al-Masih Liban
figures.description: Maronite author and scholar who studied at the Maronite school in Aleppo. Composed Syriac memre (verse homilies).

figures.name: Habash bar Jam'a
figures.description: East Syriac author who wrote a chronicle describing the Persian siege against Mosul in 1743.

figures.name: Peter of Matush
figures.description: Maronite cleric and scholar born in Cyprus. Studied and taught at the Maronite College in Rome, became a Jesuit, and authored an Arabic grammar (Institutiones linguae arabicae).

figures.name: Shemsha of Beth Saidaya
figures.description: East Syriac priest and author of liturgical poetry, including a work about the cross. A representative of later Syriac literary tradition.

figures.name: Severus Sebokht
figures.description: Scholar, astronomer, philosopher, and mathematician. Bishop of the Monastery of Qenneshre. One of the first to mention Hindu-Arabic numerals and wrote on astronomy, astrolabes, and Aristotelian logic in Syriac.

figures.name: Eusebius of Samosata
figures.description: Bishop of Samosata and defender of Nicene orthodoxy against Arianism. Friend and ally of the Cappadocian Fathers. Ordained priests and bishops during the Arian controversy. Martyred by an Arian.

figures.name: Harmonius
figures.description: Son of Bardaisan of Edessa. Composed Syriac hymns that were widely popular until Ephrem adapted their meters for orthodox Christian use.

figures.name: Marutha of Tagrit
figures.description: First Maphrian of the Syriac Orthodox Church in the Sasanian Empire. Born near Balad, became a monk at the monasteries of Mar Zakkay and Mor Matay before establishing the Maphrianate of the East.

figures.name: Simeon bar Sabba'e
figures.description: Bishop of Seleucia-Ctesiphon and one of the most famous Persian martyrs. From Susa, he succeeded Catholicos Papa bar 'Aggai. Arrested and decapitated during the persecution of Shapur II.

figures.name: Thomas of Harqel
figures.description: Bishop of Mabbug (Hierapolis), diplomat, and Bible translator. Produced the Harklean version of the Syriac New Testament, one of the most important Syriac biblical translations.

figures.name: Jacob of Nisibis
figures.description: First recorded bishop of Nisibis. Built the great church of Nisibis, was Ephrem's bishop, participated in the Council of Nicaea, and is credited with saving Nisibis from Shapur's siege through prayer.

figures.name: Julian Saba
figures.description: Famous ascetic who lived near Edessa. Had many disciples and fought against the Arians for orthodoxy in Antioch. Ephrem wrote a hymn cycle celebrating his life.

figures.name: Paul of Tella
figures.description: Syriac Orthodox bishop and translator who produced the Syro-Hexapla, a Syriac translation of Origen's Hexapla Old Testament - a landmark of Syriac biblical scholarship.

figures.name: Paul of Nisibis
figures.description: East Syriac theologian, biblical commentator, and metropolitan of Nisibis. Disciple of Mar Aba I, served as diplomatic intermediary between Persia and Byzantium.

figures.name: Job of Edessa
figures.description: Natural philosopher, translator, and physician from Edessa. Active in the early Abbasid period, contributing to the transmission of Greek scientific knowledge through Syriac.

figures.name: Mor Maron
figures.description: Charismatic hermit who lived in the Orontes River valley. Venerated as the founding father of the Maronite Church and Syriac monastic tradition in Lebanon and Syria.

figures.name: Israel of Alqosh
figures.description: East Syriac priest, poet, scholar, and scribe from Alqosh. Founder of the Shikwana family of scribes who preserved Syriac manuscripts for generations.

figures.name: Yuhannon bar Aphtonia
figures.description: Monastic founder from Edessa. Founded the monastery of Qenneshre on the Euphrates, which became the most important center of Greek-Syriac learning. Author of a Life of Severus of Antioch.

figures.name: Dadisho I the Aramean
figures.description: Catholicos of the Church of the East, explicitly called 'Dadisho the Aramean' in Syriac sources. Led the church as Bishop of Seleucia-Ctesiphon.

figures.name: Dadisho Qatraya
figures.description: East Syriac monastic author from Beth Qatraye (Persian Gulf region). Wrote on asceticism and the spiritual life.

figures.name: Enanisho
figures.description: East Syriac monk of Beth 'Abe who compiled the Syriac Paradise of the Fathers, a translation and expansion of Palladius's Lausiac History.

figures.name: Daniel bar Maryam
figures.description: Syriac author of an Ecclesiastical History.

figures.name: Elisha bar Quzbaye
figures.description: Teacher of biblical interpretation and director of the School of Nisibis. Known as 'the Interpreter' for his exegetical work.

figures.name: Emmanuel bar Shahhare
figures.description: East Syriac monk and author of a Hexaemeron (commentary on the six days of creation). Based at the Upper Monastery near Mosul.

figures.name: Elijah of Qartmin
figures.description: Monastic author at the monastery of Qartmin in Tur Abdin. Wrote a verse biography of Philoxenos of Mabbug.

figures.name: Gabriel Qatraya
figures.description: East Syriac author of an important Commentary on the Liturgy from Beth Qatraye.

figures.name: Elijah of Anbar
figures.description: Bishop of al-Anbar and composer of didactic poetry in Syriac.

figures.name: Habib of Edessa
figures.description: Syriac author from Edessa.

figures.name: Michael Badoqa
figures.description: Syriac author and exegete. Scholar and teacher at the School of Nisibis during Henana's tenure as its head (572-610).

figures.name: Henana of Adiabene
figures.description: Controversial director of the School of Nisibis who introduced new exegetical methods influenced by Greek patristic thought, causing a major split in the Church of the East.

figures.name: Hiba of Edessa
figures.description: Bishop of Edessa and translator. Central figure in the Christological controversies of the 5th century, whose letter to Mari the Persian became one of the Three Chapters.

figures.name: Sergius bar Wahle
figures.description: East Syriac monk and poet from Azerbaijan.

figures.name: Proba of Antioch
figures.description: Syriac commentator on Aristotle's writings on logic. Archdeacon of Antioch who helped transmit Greek philosophical thought into Syriac.

figures.name: Cyrus of Edessa
figures.description: Syriac author from Edessa, associated with the School of Edessa tradition.

figures.name: Stephan al-Duwayhi
figures.description: Maronite Patriarch (1670-1704) and scholar. Authored major historical and liturgical works on the Maronite Church.

figures.name: John Naqar
figures.description: Syriac Orthodox ascetic and author on the Holy Mountain near Edessa.

figures.name: Moses of Aggel
figures.description: Translator of Cyril of Alexandria's Glaphyra and of the History of Joseph and Aseneth into Syriac.

figures.name: George of al-Bsheriyyeh
figures.description: Syriac Orthodox scribe and bishop of al-Bsheriyyeh (1707-1748). Son of Abraham Abd al-Nur of Aleppo.

figures.name: Paul Bedjan
figures.description: Chaldean Catholic priest and prolific publisher of Syriac texts. Edited and published massive collections of Syriac hagiography, history, and literature that remain standard references.

figures.name: Gabriel Cardahi
figures.description: Lebanese Maronite priest and scholar. Published important collections of Syriac poetry and literature including Liber Thesauri de Arte Poetica Syrorum.

figures.name: Josephus Simonius Assemani
figures.description: Maronite polymath and Custodian of the Vatican Library. Author of the monumental Bibliotheca Orientalis, the foundational reference work for Syriac studies. Titular bishop of Tyre.

figures.name: Polycarp of Mabbug
figures.description: Chorepiscopus of Mabbug commissioned by Philoxenos to produce the Philoxenian version of the New Testament, one of the landmark Syriac biblical translations.

figures.name: Stephen bar Sudayli
figures.description: Syriac monk from Edessa to whom pantheist ideas were attributed. Likely author of the mystical Book of the Holy Hierotheos.

figures.name: Barhadbshabba Arbaya
figures.description: Member of the School of Nisibis who authored the Ecclesiastical History and the Cause of the Foundation of the Schools - key sources for the history of Syriac education.

figures.name: Rabban bar Idta
figures.description: Disciple of Abraham of Kashkar and important monastic founder who built a monastery in the region of Marga in northern Iraq.

figures.name: Abraham of Kashkar
figures.description: Founder and abbot of the Great Monastery on Mount Izla near Nisibis. Called 'Father of the Monks of the Orient,' he led a major reform of East Syriac monasticism.

figures.name: Abraham of Beth Rabban
figures.description: Teacher of biblical interpretation and director of the School of Nisibis, the most important academic institution of the Syriac tradition.

figures.name: Abraham of Nathpar
figures.description: East Syriac ascetic author from Adiabene who wrote treatises on monasticism and contemplative theology. Some of his works circulated under the name of Evagrius of Pontus.

figures.name: Aitalaha of Edessa
figures.description: Bishop of Edessa (324/5-345/6), one of the early bishops of the Syriac heartland.

figures.name: Jirjis Amira
figures.description: Maronite Patriarch and Syriac grammarian. Authored an important grammar of the Syriac language.

figures.name: Aba II of Kashkar
figures.description: Scholar, bishop of Kashkar, and Catholicos of the Church of the East (741-751).

figures.name: Aba, disciple of Ephrem
figures.description: Disciple of Ephrem the Syrian, author, and biblical commentator in the Edessa tradition.

figures.name: Abdisho bar Bahriz
figures.description: East Syriac logician, theologian, legal scholar, and translator. Metropolitan first of Harran, then of Mosul and Hazza.

figures.name: Abdullah I bar Stephanos
figures.description: Syriac Orthodox Patriarch (1521-57) and advocate for printing the first Syriac New Testament.

figures.name: Abgar the Hagiographer
figures.description: Syriac hagiographer from Beth Garmai. Author of the martyrdom of Hormizd and his nine companions who died during the reign of Yazdgard.

figures.name: Cosmas, priest of Edessa
figures.description: Disciple, correspondent, and biographer of Simeon the Stylite. One of the primary sources for Simeon's life.

figures.name: Abraham Zabaya
figures.description: East Syriac priest and author of a metrical life of Rabban Bar 'Edta.

figures.name: Sliba of Hah
figures.description: Syriac monastic author from Hah in Tur Abdin who composed a martyrology after the time of Bar Hebraeus.

figures.name: Ni'matullah Ignatius
figures.description: Syriac Orthodox scholar, astronomer, Maphrian (1555-1557) and Patriarch of Antioch (1557-1562).

figures.name: Simeon II, Maphrian of Tur Abdin
figures.description: Writer and Maphrian of Tur Abdin (1710-1740). Martyred for his faith.

figures.name: Bar Sahde of Karka
figures.description: East Syriac author from Karka de Beth Slokh (Kirkuk). Wrote a Book of Ecclesiastical History on the Himyarite Martyrs.

figures.name: Yahb Metkarkana
figures.description: Syriac author who wrote a work about Rabban Sargis.

figures.name: Thomais
figures.description: Possibly the only documented female Syriac author whose work survives. A nun who authored a Life of Febronia, claiming to have been a fellow nun with her.

figures.name: Isaiah of Arzun
figures.description: Eyewitness from Arzun and author of a hagiographic text commemorating martyrs under Shapur II of Persia.

figures.name: Jesse, priest and doctor
figures.description: Doctor of the Church of the East and interpreter at the School of Seleucia-Ctesiphon. Disciple of Mar Aba I and author of a treatise On the Commemoration of the Holy Martyrs.

figures.name: Peter the Solitary
figures.description: East Syriac monk and author of a life of Catholicos Sabrisho I.

figures.name: Paul, disciple of Aaron of Serugh
figures.description: Syriac author of the Life of Aaron of Serugh, a disciple of the monastic tradition of Serugh.

figures.name: John the Prefect
figures.description: Syriac author of a hagiographical work about the martyr Dodo.

figures.name: David Puniqoyo
figures.description: Syriac Orthodox priest, author, and poet from Homs (Emesa).

figures.name: Nuh the Lebanese
figures.description: Syriac Orthodox author, Maphrian (1489-1493) and Patriarch of Antioch (1493-1509).

figures.name: Masud of Tur Abdin
figures.description: Syriac Orthodox monk, author, and church leader from Tur Abdin. Served as abbot, bishop, and Patriarch of Antioch.

figures.name: George of Resh'ayna
figures.description: Syriac Orthodox bishop and author of an early Syriac Life of Maximus the Confessor. From Resh'ayna (Ras al-Ayn) in northern Syria.

figures.name: John the Monk
figures.description: Syriac monk and author of a historical text about Catholicos Denha I, possibly his secretary.

figures.name: John bar Shayullah
figures.description: Syriac Orthodox Patriarch born at Mardin. Composed a hagiography of David of Homs and was himself the subject of a hagiography.

figures.name: Prosdocia
figures.description: Syriac martyr from the Euphrates region who threw herself into the Euphrates rather than recant her Christian faith during a persecution.

figures.name: Berenice
figures.description: Syriac martyr who threw herself into the Euphrates together with Prosdocia and Domnina rather than recant her Christian faith.

figures.name: Domnina
figures.description: Syriac martyr who threw herself into the Euphrates together with Berenice and Prosdocia rather than recant her Christian faith.

figures.name: Behnam Hadloyo
figures.description: Syriac Orthodox Patriarch and liturgical composer.

figures.name: Daniel of Edessa
figures.description: Bishop of Edessa who commissioned the Syriac translation of the letters of Severus of Antioch, preserving a major body of Syriac theological correspondence.

figures.name: Barsoum Safi
figures.description: Younger brother of Bar Hebraeus and his successor as Maphrian of the Syriac Orthodox Church (1288-1307/8).

figures.name: Yeshu' bar Khayrun
figures.description: Syriac author born in Hah, Tur Abdin. Son of the priest Slibo bar Khayrun.

figures.name: Isaiah of Beth Sbirino
figures.description: Syriac priest and author from Tur Abdin. Composed two poems documenting the devastation caused by Tamerlane's invasions of Tur Abdin.

figures.name: Daniel of Mardin
figures.description: Syriac Orthodox monk and author from Mardin.

figures.name: Abraham II Gharib
figures.description: Syriac Orthodox liturgical writer and Patriarch of Antioch (1382-1412).

figures.name: John of Mardin
figures.description: Metropolitan of Mardin, author, and restorer of 25 monasteries and churches including the monastery of Mar Hananya (Deir al-Za'faran).

figures.name: Theodore of Antioch, the Philosopher
figures.description: Syriac philosopher from Antioch active in the 13th century.

figures.name: Metropolitan Gabriel of Bartella
figures.description: Syriac Orthodox bishop and author from Bartella (near Mosul).

figures.name: Athanasius VII
figures.description: Syriac Orthodox Patriarch, monk, and author.

figures.name: Isa b. Zur'a
figures.description: Syriac Christian philosopher and translator from Baghdad who translated Greek philosophical texts into Arabic.

figures.name: Seven Children of Beth Zabdai
figures.description: Seven Aramean martyrs from Beth Zabdai (Tur Abdin region) who were imprisoned and martyred for their faith.

figures.name: Seven Martyrs of Samosata
figures.description: Seven Aramean martyrs from Samosata - Hyperechius, Philotheus, Jacob, Paragros, Habib, Romanus, and Lollian - commemorated together in Syriac hagiography.

figures.name: Yahya b. Adi
figures.description: Syriac Christian translator, philosopher, logician, and theologian from Baghdad. Translated Greek philosophical texts into Arabic and wrote original works on logic and theology.

figures.name: al-Hasan b. Suwar Ibn al-Khammar
figures.description: Syriac Christian philosopher and translator from Baghdad. Student of Yahya b. Adi, known for his work on Aristotelian logic.

figures.name: Rupil the Monk
figures.description: Syriac Christian logician and likely professor in Baghdad. Part of the Syriac philosophical tradition of the Abbasid period.

figures.name: Denha the Philosopher
figures.description: Syriac Christian philosopher and logician active in the 10th century.

figures.name: Habib of Samosata
figures.description: Aramean martyr from Samosata, commemorated in Syriac hagiography.

figures.name: Habib
figures.description: Syriac Christian martyr commemorated alongside Zebinas, Lazarus, Maroutha, Narses, Elijah, Mahri, Saba, Berikhicho, Jonas, and Chembaiteh in Syriac hagiography.

figures.name: Hasho
figures.description: Syriac Christian martyr killed under Shah Yazdegerd I alongside companions Afrem, Abda, Jacob, Papa, Daduq, and Durtan the learned.

figures.name: Hala
figures.description: Syriac martyr commemorated in hagiographic texts preserved in the British Library (Add. 14647 and Add. 14735).

figures.name: Hapsai
figures.description: Aramean Christian martyr from Arbela (Adiabene) who was decapitated alongside Aitalaha, a former pagan priest who converted to Christianity.

figures.name: Harphat
figures.description: Syriac martyr commemorated in hagiographic texts preserved in the British Library (Add. 14647, Add. 7190, Add. 14730, Add. 14650).

figures.name: Hiran of Adiabene
figures.description: Aramean Christian martyr from Adiabene, commemorated in Syriac hagiography.

figures.name: Simeon of Nisibis
figures.description: Syriac deacon from Nisibis active in the 10th century.

figures.name: Ignatius (Patriarch)
figures.description: Syriac Orthodox patriarch and maphrian commemorated in Syriac hagiographic literature.

figures.name: Ignatius XVIII David Shah
figures.description: Syriac Orthodox Patriarch commemorated in a panegyric preserved in Syriac manuscripts.

figures.name: Ina
figures.description: Syriac Christian martyr commemorated in hagiographic literature.

figures.name: Innocent
figures.description: Syriac Christian martyr commemorated in at least four Syriac manuscripts including ms Lady Meux 6.

figures.name: Irene of Nisibis
figures.description: Noble-born Christian convert who worked as a miracle-worker in the cities of Megedo, Kallinikos, Tella, and Nisibis, and was ultimately martyred for refusing to renounce her faith.

figures.name: Isaac (martyr)
figures.description: Syriac Christian martyr commemorated in hagiographic texts preserved in the British Library (Add. 14647).

figures.name: Isaac (companion of Hasho)
figures.description: Syriac Christian martyr killed under Shah Yazdegerd I alongside companions Afrem, Abda, Jacob, Papa, Daduq, Durtan, and Hasho.

figures.name: Isaac (Syriac martyr)
figures.description: Syriac Christian martyr commemorated in Isaac and Dada, a hagiographic text preserved in British Library Add. 17202.

figures.name: Isaac, Bishop of Karka
figures.description: Bishop of Karka d-Beth Slokh martyred under Shapor II alongside Shapor, bishop of Niqator. Their names were later associated with a group of martyrs killed under Yazdgerd II.

figures.name: Isaac of Adiabene
figures.description: Aramean Christian martyr from Adiabene, commemorated in Syriac hagiographic manuscripts.

figures.name: Isaiah of Palestine
figures.description: Monk of Scetis whose writings on asceticism and the mystical life were foundational for the Syriac monastic tradition, transmitted via the Syriac translation of the Paradise of the Fathers.

figures.name: ʿAbdishoʿ (teacher of Mar Qardagh)
figures.description: Syriac Christian teacher of Mar Qardagh, the Assyrian martyr-king, in the East Syriac hagiographic tradition.

figures.name: Zaytun of Anhil
figures.description: Syriac Orthodox Metropolitan of Anhil who died in 1855.

figures.name: Theodosius the Patriarch
figures.description: Syriac Orthodox Patriarch of Antioch (887-896), author, and physician. Also known as Romanos the physician.

figures.name: Dourtan
figures.description: Syriac Christian martyr killed under Shah Yazdegerd I alongside companions Afrem, Abda, Jacob, Papa, Daduq, Hasho, and Isaac.

figures.name: ʿEbed-Mshiha of Adiabene
figures.description: Aramean Christian martyr from Adiabene, commemorated in Syriac hagiographic manuscripts.

figures.name: Isaac of Amid
figures.description: Syriac priest and writer from Amid (Diyarbakir). Known also as Isaac of Antioch. A prolific author of Syriac verse and prose homilies.

figures.name: Zʿura of Nisibis
figures.description: Syriac deacon from Nisibis active in the medieval period.

figures.name: Elijah of Dara
figures.description: Syriac martyr from Dara, an Aramean city in the Tur Abdin region, commemorated in hagiographic texts preserved in the British Library (Add. 14647).

figures.name: Garshun the Stranger
figures.description: Syriac author active in the late 10th and early 11th century.

figures.name: Job of Manʿem
figures.description: Syriac scholar active in the 9th century.

figures.name: Euphemia of Edessa
figures.description: Aramean woman from Edessa (Urhoy) whose story is set in the Syriac tradition. Enslaved by a Goth after being given to him in marriage, she was miraculously rescued and returned to Edessa through the intercession of the Syriac martyrs Shmona, Guria, and Habib.

figures.name: Eustathius, Bishop of Antioch
figures.description: Bishop of Antioch who fiercely opposed Arianism at the Council of Nicaea and was a staunch defender of Nicene Christianity.

figures.name: Moses bar Kipho
figures.description: Syriac Orthodox Bishop of Beth Raman on the Tigris, prolific theologian and author. Monk of the monastery of Saint Sergius near Balad. Wrote on many theological and scientific topics and was influential in the Maphrianate of Tagrit.

figures.name: Gaddai
figures.description: Syriac martyr commemorated in at least five manuscripts including ms Lady Meux 6.

figures.name: Dionysios II
figures.description: Syriac Orthodox Patriarch who died in 909.

figures.name: Aaron of Serugh
figures.description: Disciple of Mar Awgin and founder of two monasteries near Melitene. From Serugh (Suruç) in the Aramean heartland.

figures.name: Aba of Nineveh
figures.description: Bishop of Nineveh martyred under Shah Shapur II.

figures.name: Abai of Hah
figures.description: Monk, miracle-worker, and disciple of Simeon of Qartmin from Hah in Tur Abdin. Became abbot of the monastery of Qartmin and helped end a plague through his prayers.

figures.name: ʿAbda of Edessa
figures.description: Bishop of Edessa (Urhoy), the Aramean city that was a major center of early Syriac Christianity.

figures.name: ʿAbda of Hormizd Ardashir
figures.description: Bishop of Hormizd Ardashir martyred under Yazdegerd I alongside companions Afrem, Jacob, Papa, Daduq, and Durtan the learned.

figures.name: Ephrem the Scribe
figures.description: Syriac Christian scribe and martyr killed under Shah Yazdegerd I alongside companions ʿAbda, Jacob, Papa the deacon, Daduq, and Durtan the learned.

figures.name: ʿAbdā Alaha
figures.description: Syriac Christian priest tortured alongside ʿAbdishoʿ of Kashkar by Ardashir, brother of Shapur. Arrested with seven friends and seven virgins and martyred with 38 companions.

figures.name: Basil of Emesa
figures.description: Bishop of Emesa (Homs), an ancient Aramean city in Syria.

figures.name: ʿAbdishoʿ of Kashkar
figures.description: Syriac Christian martyr from Kashkar, martyred alongside the priest ʿAbdā Alaha by Ardashir, brother of Shapur. Executed with 38 companions.

figures.name: Abel of Qartmin
figures.description: First stylite saint of the monastery of Qartmin in Tur Abdin. Patron against eye disease and paralysis. Philoxenus of Mabbug sought his benediction.

figures.name: Abhai
figures.description: Ascetic featured in John of Ephesus' Lives of the Eastern Saints. Ordained Bishop of Nicaea and founder of the Monastery of the Oaks.

figures.name: Abimelech of Nisibis
figures.description: Theologian of the School of Balad who became founder of the martyrion, a secondary institution of the School of Nisibis.

figures.name: Abraham, Bishop of Arbela
figures.description: Bishop of Arbela in Adiabene martyred under Shah Shapur II.

figures.name: Abraham of the High Mountain
figures.description: Monk and miracle-worker of the monastery of the High Mountain north of Mount Izla. Teacher of Bar Sauma and founder of the monastery of Mor Gabriel near Midyat in Tur Abdin.

figures.name: Abraham of Beth Sayyare
figures.description: Monk from the family of Mar Awgin and Abraham the Great. Founded a monastery at Zawitha, west of Bamarne, in the Aramean monastic tradition.

figures.name: Abraham the Scribe
figures.description: Monk of the monastery of Qartmin in Tur Abdin known for curing lepers. Also known as Abraham of Shawur.

figures.name: Abraham Qidounaya
figures.description: Syriac anchorite whose niece Mary fell from the ascetic life but was redeemed through his love. A beloved figure in Syriac hagiographic tradition.

figures.name: Abshelama of Edessa
figures.description: Early bishop of Edessa and copyist for the Apostle Addai. According to the Teaching of Addai, he was among the first Christian leaders of the Aramean city of Edessa.

figures.name: Addai the Chorepiscos
figures.description: Monk and chorepiscopus commemorated in John of Ephesus' Lives of the Eastern Saints.

figures.name: Addai the Monk
figures.description: Syriac monk commemorated by John of Ephesus in his Lives of the Eastern Saints. Built twelve monasteries together with his brother Abraham.

figures.name: Addai the Apostle
figures.description: One of the 72 apostles, sent as a missionary to Edessa (Urhoy). Healed King Abgar V and converted the Aramean city of Edessa to Christianity, as recorded in the Teaching of Addai. Foundational figure of Syriac Christianity.

figures.name: Simeon of Qenneshre
figures.description: Presbyter of the monastery of Qenneshrin, one of the great centers of Aramean Syriac learning and scholarship.

figures.name: Adorparwa
figures.description: Aramean martyr of Tur Berʿain in Beth Garmai, commemorated with his brother Mirnarsai and sister Sultan Mahduk.

figures.name: Aggai, Bishop of Edessa
figures.description: Ordained by the Apostle Addai to be bishop of Edessa. Martyred by the son of King Abgar, becoming one of the earliest martyrs of Syriac Christianity.

figures.name: Aha of Arzun
figures.description: Bishop of Arzun and Miaphysite missionary saint among the Armenians.

figures.name: Aha the Solitary
figures.description: Former soldier from Resh ʿAyna (an Aramean city) who founded a monastery near Nisibis, undertook extensive pilgrimages, and returned with a piece of the True Cross. Converted a village of pagan Armenians.

figures.name: Amai of Adiabene
figures.description: Daughter of the covenant from Adiabene, martyred alongside Thecla and other daughters of the covenant.

figures.name: ʿAmmi of Hah
figures.description: First bishop of Tur ʿAbdin. Disciple of Simeon of Qartmin, from Hah in Tur Abdin. Martyred in Tanzi.

figures.name: Jacob of Edessa
figures.description: Bishop of Edessa (684-708), greatest Syriac Orthodox biblical scholar and polymath. Joined the monastery of Qenneshre, studied in Alexandria and Edessa, and wrote commentaries on scripture, grammar, and philosophy. Died at the monastery of Tell ʿAda.

figures.name: ʿAqebshma of Adiabene
figures.description: Bishop from Adiabene martyred with Joseph and Ithalaha during the persecution of Shapur II. Buried by an Armenian princess.

figures.name: Archelaus of Harran
figures.description: Bishop of Harran, the ancient Aramean city. Known for his debate with the Manichaean founder Mani.

figures.name: Athanasius of Tur Abdin
figures.description: Monk of Tur ʿAbdin in the Aramean heartland, also known as Rabban Sliba.

figures.name: Euthalius the Bishop
figures.description: Syriac Orthodox bishop active in the 8th century.

figures.name: Athanasius of Qenneshrin
figures.description: Bishop from Qenneshrin, the renowned Aramean Syriac monastery and seat of learning.

figures.name: Athanasius Sandalaya
figures.description: West Syriac Metropolitan of Maypherqat who constructed a monastery at Tel Besme, west of Mardin.

figures.name: Athqen of Sis
figures.description: Monk from Sis (Iraq) who came northward to Mount Izla and became the third superior of the monastery of Rabban Saliba.

figures.name: ʿAbdishoʿ of Arbela
figures.description: Anchorite monk from near Arbela (Adiabene) who converted the soldier-saint Mar Qardagh to Christianity.

figures.name: ʿAbdishoʿ of Kashkar (bishop)
figures.description: Bishop and martyr of Kashkar, an Aramean city in Iraq.

figures.name: Azad of Adiabene
figures.description: Deacon of Beth Naggare in Adiabene martyred with the priest Jacob during the persecution of Shapur II.

figures.name: Azad (eunuch of Shapur II)
figures.description: Eunuch at the court of Shapur II who converted to Christianity and was martyred at the gate of the palace of Karka d-Ledan, a week after Simeon Bar Sabbaʿe.

figures.name: Babai of Edessa
figures.description: Sister of the Edessan martyr Sharbel and a convert from paganism. Martyred in Edessa during the reign of Emperor Trajan.

figures.name: Babylas of Antioch
figures.description: Bishop of Antioch (237-250) who famously demanded that Emperor Philip the Arab make public penance. Died from mistreatment in prison and venerated as a martyr.

figures.name: Badai the Priest
figures.description: Syriac Christian priest and martyr who was flagellated with pomegranate branches at the command of Mihrnarsai.

figures.name: Barbaʿshmin of Seleucia-Ctesiphon
figures.description: Bishop and martyr of Seleucia-Ctesiphon. Arrested at Karka d-Ledan and martyred during the persecution of Shapur II.

figures.name: Barbʿashmin (Patriarch)
figures.description: Syriac Orthodox Patriarch commemorated in the Syriac hagiographic tradition.

figures.name: Barhadbshabba of Arbela
figures.description: Deacon of Arbela (Adiabene) condemned to death and martyred during the persecution of Shapur II.

figures.name: Simeon of Samosata
figures.description: Presbyter of Samosata, the ancient Aramean city on the Euphrates.

figures.name: Barhadbshabba of Qartmin
figures.description: Monk and disciple of Samuel of Qartmin at the monastery of Qartmin in Tur Abdin.

figures.name: Barsai of Harran
figures.description: Bishop of Harran and then Edessa during the time of Ephrem the Syrian. Built the Grand Baptistery in Edessa.

figures.name: Barsamya of Edessa
figures.description: Early Bishop of Edessa during the reign of Emperor Trajan. Contemporary of the Edessan martyrs Sharbel and Babai.

figures.name: Barsauma of Hashrai
figures.description: Bishop and martyr of the monastery of Hashrai in Tur ʿAbdin.

figures.name: Bassus
figures.description: Son of a Zoroastrian governor who converted to Christianity with his twin sister Susan through a Christian slave. Martyred by their father. A monastery commemorating Mar Bassus was founded near Apamea in Aramean Syria.

figures.name: Susan
figures.description: Twin sister of Bassus. Daughter of a Zoroastrian governor who converted to Christianity with her brother and was martyred by their father.

figures.name: Bawai the Catholicos
figures.description: Zoroastrian convert who became Catholicos of the Church of the East. Born in Tella (Aramean city), he became a monk and was elected patriarch. Killed, reportedly due to accusations by his rival Barsauma.

figures.name: David of Germanicea
figures.description: Bishop of Germanicea (Marʿash/Kahramanmaraş), a city in the Aramean region of northern Syria.

figures.name: Behnam of Kirkuk
figures.description: Son of the covenant from the Kirkuk region martyred under Shah Ardashir II.

figures.name: Behnam of Mosul
figures.description: High-born Christian martyr, son of Sennacherib, who converted to Christianity through the monk Mattai and was martyred by his father near Mosul. His father later repented and built monasteries for Mar Mattai and Abraham near Mosul.

figures.name: Benjamin the Deacon
figures.description: Syriac Christian deacon and martyr under Vahram V.

figures.name: Benjamin of Dara
figures.description: Hermit and priest from Dara in Tur Abdin, ordained by Barsai of Edessa. Travelled to Mount Sinjar and converted Maʿin; both Benjamin and Maʿin were martyred.

figures.name: Benjamin, disciple of Mar Awgin
figures.description: Disciple of Mar Awgin who travelled to Mount Izla and founded a monastery and school near Mardin in the Aramean heartland.

figures.name: Bohtishoʿ the Deacon
figures.description: Syriac Christian deacon and martyr who assisted Tomarsha in rebuilding churches destroyed under Shapur II. Martyred under Vahram.

figures.name: Bohtizad of Kurke
figures.description: Syriac saint from Kurke with a monastery named after him in the mountains of northeastern Iraq.

figures.name: Brikhishoʿ
figures.description: Syriac Christian martyr who died with ten companions during the time of Shapur II.

figures.name: Brihishoʿ of Beth Asa
figures.description: Brother of Yawnan. Two brothers from Beth Asa who travelled to a neighboring village to encourage Christian martyrs and were themselves martyred during the time of Shapur.

figures.name: Moses of Anhil
figures.description: Syriac Orthodox historian active in the 8th century.

figures.name: Buya, Rabban
figures.description: Monk from ʿAqra in Iraq with many companions. His anonymous sister was also venerated as a saint with her tomb in Shaqlawa.

figures.name: Carpus of Tur Abdin
figures.description: Bishop of Shawaur martyred by the Persians. His relics were placed inside a church in Tur ʿAbdin built by Saliba, father of Samuel of Qartmin.

figures.name: Christina Yazdoi
figures.description: Daughter of a Zoroastrian governor from Karka d-Beth Slokh who converted to Christianity and was martyred after her marriage.

figures.name: Cyprian of Antioch
figures.description: Martyr from Antioch, the great Aramean city, who died with Justina under Emperor Diocletian.

figures.name: Cyrus, Bishop of Edessa
figures.description: Bishop of Edessa who transferred the relics of the Apostle Thomas to Edessa in 394 AD.

figures.name: Cyrus of Harran
figures.description: Martyr of Harran, the ancient Aramean city, killed under the Abbasid Caliph Al-Mansur.

figures.name: Cyrus of Qartmin
figures.description: Superior of the monastery of Qartmin in Tur Abdin. Disciple of Samuel of Qartmin.

figures.name: Cyriacus (disciple of Mar Yareth)
figures.description: Syriac disciple of Mar Yareth.

figures.name: Dodo of Tur ʿAbdin
figures.description: Saint from Tur ʿAbdin and companion of Mar Awgin. A church in Beth Sbirino is dedicated to him.

figures.name: Dado
figures.description: Convert from Zoroastrianism to Christianity. Condemned to an ordeal of fire and martyred under Shapur II.

figures.name: Damian, Patriarch of Alexandria
figures.description: Patriarch of Alexandria of Syrian origin. Lived as a monastic ascetic in Egypt before becoming patriarch. Involved in disputes with Peter of Callinicus over the Tritheist controversy.

figures.name: Daniel of Amida
figures.description: Refugee from Amida (Diyarbakir) and student of Mar Mattai. Established a monastery called the monastery of the yellow source near his teacher's monastery.

figures.name: Daniel of Galash
figures.description: Syriac ascetic who visited the portrait of Christ in Edessa, met Julian Saba, and established a monastery on Mount Aysum.

figures.name: Daniel, Bishop of Edessa
figures.description: Bishop of Edessa who obtained relics of Severus of Samosata to chase demons from monks at Qenneshre. Wrote a demonology.

figures.name: Daniel the Doctor
figures.description: Convert from paganism who travelled to Nuhadra in the Aramean region. Healed Miles, the son of a Persian governor, and lived as a hermit.

figures.name: Daniel of Qartmin
figures.description: Monk of Qartmin in Tur Abdin who was elected bishop of Qartmin.

figures.name: Daniel the Stylite (of Qartmin)
figures.description: Monk and disciple of Samuel of Qartmin who walked along the Tigris to the land of Qardu (Gazarta).

figures.name: David of Harran
figures.description: Bishop of Harran, originally a monk from Qartmin and a relative of Simeon of the Olives. Left his precious objects including a collection of canons to the monastery of Qartmin.

figures.name: Demetrianus of Antioch
figures.description: Bishop of Antioch deported by the Persians after their conquest of the city in 256. The beginnings of the diocese of Gundishapur were attributed to him.

figures.name: Ten Brothers of Qartmin
figures.description: Group of ten monks from the monastery of Qartmin in Tur Abdin who fought with villagers over the body of Simeon of Qartmin.

figures.name: Domitius
figures.description: Syriac martyr and doctor from Kurdistan venerated near Qilleth. Either a hermit martyred in his cave or a doctor who gave counsel to Emperor Valens.

figures.name: Edna
figures.description: Saint widely venerated among Maronite Christians. Her name means 'ear' and she is invoked for ear infections.

figures.name: Elian of Emesa
figures.description: Aramean martyr and doctor from Emesa (Homs). Executed by his own father. The bishop Paul built a church in his honor.

figures.name: Elijah, Bishop of ʿAyn Ward
figures.description: First bishop from the monastery of Simeon of Qartmin. Bishop of ʿAyn Ward.

figures.name: George, Bishop of the Arabs
figures.description: Student of Severus of Sebokht at Qenneshre, versed in all branches of knowledge. Became Bishop of the Arab tribes in 686 with his seat in Aqula.

figures.name: Elijah, Patriarch of Antioch
figures.description: Syrian Orthodox Patriarch of Antioch and convert from the Melkite community. Originally a monk from the monastery of Gubba Barraya. Esteemed by Caliph Al-Walid I who allowed him to build a church.

figures.name: Elijah the Younger of Damascus
figures.description: Martyr from Damascus, the ancient Aramean capital, celebrated on February 1.

figures.name: Elisha of Garbiya
figures.description: Monk of Garbiya near Midyat in Tur Abdin.

figures.name: Stephen (companion of Bassus)
figures.description: Syriac martyr commemorated with Bassus, Suzanna, and Longinus.

figures.name: Eulogius (disciple of Mar Awgin)
figures.description: Syriac ascetic and disciple of Mar Awgin, known as 'Eulogius and the leper.'

figures.name: Eutal of Magdala
figures.description: Pagan convert who became a monk with Mar Aba in Mopsuestia. A miracle-worker who converted thousands of pagans.

figures.name: Eutychios the Mesopotamian
figures.description: Mesopotamian martyr under Caliph Al-Walid who died for refusing to convert to Islam.

figures.name: Ezekiel the Monk
figures.description: Disciple of Mar Awgin who went to Adiabene and Beth Garmai. Converted many Zoroastrians and founded a monastery near Daduq in the Kirkuk region.

figures.name: Febronia of Nisibis
figures.description: Aramean nun and martyr from a convent near Nisibis. Renowned for her beauty, learning, asceticism, and bravery. Martyred for refusing to marry a pagan statesman.

figures.name: Gabriel of Qartmin
figures.description: From Beth Qustan, became Bishop of Qartmin. Fled marriage to become a monk, was superior of Qartmin, and met the Caliph Ibn al-Hattab. Set out measurements of the monastery.

figures.name: Gabriel of Kashkar
figures.description: Syriac monk known as 'the little man' who founded three monasteries near Mahoze, Dayr Qunni, and Husra.

figures.name: Gabrona of Qarta
figures.description: Syriac monk from Beth ʿArabaye who healed the daughter of a village leader and constructed the monastery of Dayr al-Qara.

figures.name: Ganni of Hirta
figures.description: Monk from Beth Aramaye ('house of Arameans') who sold all possessions and became a disciple of Mar Abraham on Mount Izla. Praised by Simeon of Taybutha for his virtues.

figures.name: George of Harran
figures.description: Bishop of Harran who came from the monastery of Qartmin.

figures.name: Simeon of the Olives
figures.description: Syriac Orthodox saint and relative of David of Harran.

figures.name: George the Priest of Izla
figures.description: Monk of Izla and convert from Zoroastrianism. Noted for his conversations with the Monophysites. Condemned to death by Shah Khusro for leaving Zoroastrianism.

figures.name: Gourya of Edessa
figures.description: Aramean martyr killed in Edessa during the Diocletian persecution alongside Shmona. The subject of great devotion in Edessa.

figures.name: Habib of Edessa
figures.description: Deacon from the village of Telshaha near Edessa. Continued traveling from village to village encouraging Christians during persecution. Burnt to death, with his mother accompanying him. Entombed near Shmona and Guria.

figures.name: Habib (disciple of Jacob of Serugh)
figures.description: Disciple of Jacob of Serugh, the great Syriac poet.

figures.name: Habib son of Gamaliel
figures.description: Possibly identified with John of Gamaliel mentioned in the life of Samuel of Qartmin.

figures.name: Ananias of Arbela
figures.description: Aramean layman from Arbela (Adiabene) arrested in year six of the persecution of Shapur. Martyred three times. A church was dedicated to him in Erbil.

figures.name: Hananya of Dayr al-Zaʿfaran
figures.description: Syriac Orthodox bishop of Mardin and Kfartuto. Built the monastery named after him (Deir al-Zaʿfaran) on the ruins of the monastery of Slemun.

figures.name: Heliodorus of Beth Zabdai
figures.description: Bishop of Beth Zabdai in the Aramean region. 9000 inhabitants of his city were deported to Persia, and many of his community were later martyred.

figures.name: Heraclas of Kafar Sama
figures.description: Recluse from the village of Midyat in Tur Abdin.

figures.name: Hormizd of Beth Garmai
figures.description: Martyr of Beth Garmai under Yazdegerd. With nine friends, all converts from Zoroastrianism or with Zoroastrian wives, they were tortured to death.

figures.name: Rabban Hormizd
figures.description: Monastic founder of the Church of the East. Spent 32 years at the monastery of Bar ʿIdta, then founded an important monastery near Mosul, north of Alqosh.

figures.name: Hudahwi
figures.description: Syriac monk who built the monastery of Beth Hale shortly after the Muslim conquest.

figures.name: Hwara, son of Theodore
figures.description: Cured of being mute by the monk Mar Aha. Became a monk and established monasteries near Nisibis, where he was the successor of Mar Aha.

figures.name: Ia of Beth Zabdai
figures.description: Aramean woman among the martyrs of Beth Zabdai who converted the wives of Zoroastrians and was tortured and martyred.

figures.name: Ignatius of Melitene
figures.description: Bishop of Melitene who built the convent of the Mother of God and a great church there.

figures.name: Isaac, Patriarch of Harran
figures.description: Became bishop of Harran and later Patriarch. Killed by Caliph Al-Mansur and his body thrown into the Euphrates.

figures.name: Isaiah, Bishop of Edessa
figures.description: Bishop of Edessa named with the approval of the Persians who occupied the city. Refused communion to Emperor Heraclius on account of his support for Chalcedon.

figures.name: Isaiah of Aleppo
figures.description: From Aleppo, said to be the last survivor of the disciples of Mar Awgin. He and his wife lived in continence. Travelled throughout Mesopotamia and converted 3000 Marcionites.

figures.name: Isidore of Harran
figures.description: Bishop of Harran in the 7th century.

figures.name: Ishoʿsabran of Erbil
figures.description: Zoroastrian convert from Erbil (Adiabene) whose life was written by Ishoʿyaw III of Adiabene. His story speaks of interactions between the Church of the East and Syrian Orthodox Church.

figures.name: Ishoʿyahb of Mount Izla
figures.description: Monk of Mount Izla who founded a convent and healed many people.

figures.name: Ishoʿyahb of Arzun
figures.description: Patriarch of the Church of the East from Arzun.

figures.name: Ishoʿyahb of Gdala
figures.description: East Syriac patriarch from Gdala.

figures.name: Ishoʿyahb bar Qusre
figures.description: Monk from a monastery in Adiabene who founded a church that became the church of Mar Ishaʿya and residence of the metropolitan of Mosul.

figures.name: John bar Samuel
figures.description: Syriac scholar active in the 8th century.

figures.name: Israel of Kashkar
figures.description: Bishop of Kashkar elected patriarch of the Church of the East. Assassinated during the performance of the liturgy in 872.

figures.name: Aitalaha the Deacon
figures.description: Deacon martyred with Bishop ʿAqebshma during the persecution of Shapur II.

figures.name: Aitalaha, Bishop of Edessa
figures.description: Bishop from Edessa who attended the Council of Nicaea. Built the church of Cyrus and Saʿad.

figures.name: Aitalaha of Arbela
figures.description: Former pagan priest from Arbela who converted to Christianity. Imprisoned with other Persian martyrs and decapitated at Beth Lapat.

figures.name: Caesarea
figures.description: Syriac saint commemorated in John of Ephesus' Lives of the Eastern Saints.

figures.name: Shembaiteh
figures.description: Syriac Christian martyr commemorated alongside Zebinas, Lazarus, Maroutha, Narses, Elijah, Mahri, Habib, Saba, Berikhicho, and Jonas.

figures.name: Daniel of Beth Batin
figures.description: Syriac scholar (Malphono) from Beth Batin.

figures.name: Cosmos
figures.description: Twin medical saint and martyr from Syria, commemorated alongside his brother Damian.

figures.name: Damian
figures.description: Twin medical saint and martyr from Syria, commemorated alongside his brother Cosmos.

figures.name: Isaac of Nisibis (Compiler of the Anaphora)
figures.description: Syriac scholar from Nisibis known as the Compiler of the Anaphora.

figures.name: Cyriacus (Lives of the Eastern Saints)
figures.description: Syriac saint commemorated in John of Ephesus' Lives of the Eastern Saints alongside Abraham, Barhadbeshabba, and Sergius.

figures.name: Dada
figures.description: Syriac Christian saint known as a doctor of the Church, commemorated with Isaac.

figures.name: Dadouq
figures.description: Syriac Christian martyr killed under Shah Yazdegerd I alongside companions Abda, Hasho, Isaac, Afrem, Papa, and Durtan the learned.

figures.name: John III (IV)
figures.description: Syriac Orthodox Patriarch who died in 873.

figures.name: Daniel (companion of Mari and Sergius)
figures.description: Syriac martyr commemorated alongside Mari and Sergius in hagiographic texts preserved in the British Library (Add. 14647).

figures.name: Daniel of Adiabene
figures.description: Aramean Christian martyr from Adiabene, commemorated in Syriac hagiographic manuscripts.

figures.name: Ignatius II
figures.description: Syriac Orthodox Patriarch who died in 883.

figures.name: ʿAbshmayya of Edessa
figures.description: Syriac priest from Edessa (Urhoy) active in the 4th century.

figures.name: Denha of Midyat
figures.description: Priest-philosopher and monk in the Monastery of St. George in Midyat, Tur Abdin. Author of a lengthy treatise in heptasyllable meter against the heretics.

figures.name: John, Metropolitan of Dara
figures.description: Syriac author and metropolitan of Dara, the Aramean city in the Tur Abdin region.

figures.name: Jacob of ʿAnah
figures.description: Bishop of ʿAnah on the Euphrates in Aramean Mesopotamia.

figures.name: Baboi
figures.description: Patriarch of the Church of the East during the reign of Sasanian Shah Peroz.

figures.name: Barhadbshabba (Lives of the Eastern Saints)
figures.description: Syriac saint commemorated in John of Ephesus' Lives of the Eastern Saints alongside Abraham, Cyriacus, and Sergius.

figures.name: Barsauma
figures.description: Syriac saint commemorated in hagiographic texts preserved in the British Library (Add. 14592).

figures.name: Basil the Maphrian
figures.description: Syriac Orthodox Maphrian commemorated alongside Ignatius the Patriarch.

figures.name: Simeon of Hisn Mansur
figures.description: Syriac monk from Hisn Mansur (Adıyaman) in the Aramean region.

figures.name: Benjamin of Beth Nuhadra
figures.description: Syriac saint from Beth Nuhadra in the Aramean region of northern Iraq.

figures.name: Severus of Edessa
figures.description: Syriac monk of the Monastery of Saint Barbara, also known as Severus of Antioch. Active in Edessa.

figures.name: Tataq the Servant
figures.description: Chamberlain of Yazdegerd I from Adiabene. Decapitated for his Christian faith.

figures.name: Thecla
figures.description: Aramean daughter of the covenant who was arrested, interrogated, and martyred alongside her companions including Mary.

figures.name: Theodore of Kashkar
figures.description: Monk who founded his own school outside of Kashkar. In old age he retired in solitude. Went to Caliph Umar I to obtain tax exemption for priests and deacons.

figures.name: Asuna
figures.description: Syriac saint active in the 4th century.

figures.name: Theodosius, Metropolitan of Edessa
figures.description: Metropolitan bishop of Edessa, author, and translator.

figures.name: Theodosius (Bishop of Qartmin)
figures.description: Bishop and perhaps monk from Qartmin who was martyred in an oven along with his companions.

figures.name: Thomas, Bishop of Harran
figures.description: Bishop of Harran and disciple of Simeon of the Olives.

figures.name: Thomas the Stylite of Tella
figures.description: Stylite saint of Tella, an Aramean city.

figures.name: Thuthael of Edessa
figures.description: Early Aramean martyr of Edessa commemorated alongside the martyr Sharbel.

figures.name: Thuthael (Stylite of Qartmin)
figures.description: Stylite and disciple of Samuel of Qartmin in the monastery of Qartmin, Tur Abdin.

figures.name: Timothy, Bishop of Edessa
figures.description: Bishop of Edessa who participated in a synod in Mabbug that elected the deacon George.

figures.name: Yareth
figures.description: Monk trained in the monastery of Pachomius who joined Mar Awgin on Mount Izla. Converted the region of Beth Zabdai and built a monastery there with his disciple Quryaqos.

figures.name: Rabban Jonah
figures.description: Monk of the monastery of Bar Tura.

figures.name: Jonah of Anbar
figures.description: Disciple of Mar Awgin who journeyed to Jerusalem and Scetis. Founded the monastery at Peroz Shapur on the Euphrates.
